draft.title: Appeasement
card: Appeasement was the policy of giving in to some demands of an aggressive state to avoid war. Britain and France used it towards Hitler's Germany in the 1930s.
At Munich in September 1938, Britain and France agreed that Germany could take the Sudetenland, a border region of Czechoslovakia. Czechoslovakia was not a party to the decision.
Supporters of the policy point to the memory of the huge losses of World War I, public fear of another war, and the time it gave Britain and France to rearm.
Critics argue that it encouraged Hitler to demand more. Historians still debate whether appeasement was a mistake, because they weigh these arguments differently.
draft.remember: Appeasement traded concessions for peace, and historians still disagree on whether it was a mistake.

a.q: What was the main aim of Britain and France in appeasing Hitler?
opts: To avoid another war by meeting some of his demands
To help Germany rebuild its army after World War I
To make Czechoslovakia stronger against Germany
To prepare an immediate attack on Germany
a.why: Appeasement meant giving in to some demands in the hope of keeping the peace. Helping Germany rearm was not the aim, even though rearmament happened in the 1930s.
a.clue: Think about what the policy was meant to prevent.

b.q: A historian argues that the Munich agreement was a mistake. Which argument would best support this view?
opts: It encouraged Hitler to make further demands
It gave Britain and France time to rearm
It reflected public fear of another war
It was agreed with Czechoslovakia's full consent
b.why: The claim that concessions encouraged Hitler to demand more is the criticism of appeasement. Gaining time to rearm is an argument used by supporters, so it does not show the policy was a mistake.
b.clue: Which argument says the policy made things worse rather than better?

a.best: To avoid another war by meeting some of his demands

b.best: It encouraged Hitler to make further demands
